notes.title: Key facts by topic
notes.html:
Functions & transformations

  • Input and output — A function is a rule that turns every input into exactly one output, like a vending machine: press B4 and you always get the same snack.
  • Function notation — f(x) is read “f of x”. It means: use the rule f on the number x. To find f(4), put 4 into the rule.
  • Tables, graphs and the vertical line test — A graph shows a function if no vertical line touches it twice. If one input had two outputs, the machine would be broken.

Quadratics & complex numbers

  • Squares and square roots — A square with side s has area s². Going backwards, √(s²) = s. Every positive number has two square roots, one positive and one negative.
  • Solving by factoring — If two numbers multiply to zero, one of them must be zero. So (x − p)(x − q) = 0 means x = p or x = q.
  • Vertex form — y = a(x − h)² + k has its turning point at (h, k). It opens up if a > 0 and down if a < 0.

Polynomials

  • Powers and terms — x³ means x · x · x. A term is a number times powers of x. A polynomial is a sum of terms. Its degree is the highest power.
  • Adding and multiplying polynomials — Combine like terms to add. To multiply, give every term in the first factor a turn with every term in the second.
  • Evaluating and the remainder theorem — When you divide f(x) by (x − a), the remainder is f(a). So plugging in a number is a shortcut for division.

Rational functions

  • Fractions are division — A fraction a/b means a ÷ b. You can simplify by dividing the top and bottom by the same number, like 12/18 = 2/3.
  • Rational expressions — A rational expression is a polynomial divided by a polynomial. Simplify by factoring and cancelling common factors, never by cancelling terms that are added.
  • Values that are not allowed — The denominator can never be 0. Every x that makes it 0 is left out of the domain.

Exponential functions

  • Repeated multiplication — 2⁵ means 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32. The small raised number counts how many times the base is used.
  • Doubling and tripling — If a plant doubles every day, after n days it is 2ⁿ times bigger. This kind of growth starts slowly and then explodes.
  • Exponential functions — y = a·bˣ. a is the starting amount and b is the growth factor. If b > 1 it grows. If 0 < b < 1 it decays.

Logarithms

  • What a logarithm asks — log₂ 8 asks: what power of 2 gives 8? The answer is 3 because 2³ = 8. A log is an exponent in disguise.
  • Common logs — log without a base means base 10. log 1000 = 3. Each +1 means ten times bigger.
  • Special values — log_b 1 = 0 and log_b b = 1, for any base.

Sequences & series

  • Patterns and sequences — A sequence is an ordered list that follows a rule, like 3, 6, 9, 12, … Each number is a term.
  • Arithmetic sequences — You add the same amount (the common difference d) each time. The nth term is aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d.
  • Geometric sequences — You multiply by the same number (the common ratio r) each time. aₙ = a₁·rⁿ⁻¹.

Right triangles & the unit circle

  • Turns and degrees — A full turn is 360°. Half a turn is 180°, a quarter turn is 90°. The three angles of any triangle always add to 180°.
  • The sides of a right triangle — In a right triangle the longest side, across from the right angle, is the hypotenuse. For an angle you pick, the other two sides are the opposite and the adjacent.
  • Sine, cosine and tangent — SOH-CAH-TOA: sin = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tan = opposite ÷ adjacent. They are ratios, so they do not depend on how big the triangle is.

Graphs of trig functions

  • Waves in everyday life — Sound, light, tides and alternating current all repeat in smooth waves. Sine and cosine are the mathematical models for these waves.
  • The sine graph — y = sin x starts at 0, rises to 1 at 90°, returns to 0 at 180°, falls to −1 at 270°, and repeats every 360°.
  • Amplitude — The amplitude is the distance from the midline to a peak. In y = a·sin x it is |a|.

Laws of sines & cosines, vectors

  • Triangles that are not right — Many real triangles have no right angle. The Law of Sines and Law of Cosines work for every triangle.
  • Law of Sines — a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use it when you know an angle and its opposite side.
  • Law of Cosines — c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C. It is the Pythagorean theorem with a correction term. If C = 90° the correction vanishes.

Conic sections

  • Distance and midpoint — The distance between two points is a Pythagorean theorem in disguise: √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). The midpoint averages the coordinates.
  • Circles — A circle is every point the same distance r from a center (h, k): (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r².
  • Parabolas — A parabola is every point equally far from a point (the focus) and a line (the directrix). y = ax² has its focus at (0, 1/(4a)).

Polar & parametric

  • Two ways to name a point — Rectangular coordinates give (x, y). Polar coordinates give (r, θ): how far from the origin and at what angle.
  • Converting polar to rectangular — x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ.
  • Converting rectangular to polar — r = √(x² + y²) and tan θ = y/x (check the quadrant).

cards: A rule that gives each input exactly one output.
A function that undoes another: swaps inputs and outputs.
b² − 4ac; tells how many real roots a quadratic has.
A sum of terms that are numbers times whole-number powers of x.
An input where the function equals 0.
Dividing f(x) by (x − a) leaves remainder f(a).
(x − a) is a factor of f exactly when f(a) = 0.
written: Explain why dividing by zero is not allowed.
If a ÷ 0 = b, then b × 0 = a. But anything times 0 is 0, so no number b works unless a is 0, and then every b works. The answer is either impossible or not unique.
Why does a polynomial of degree n have at most n roots?
Each root gives a linear factor (x − r). Degree n allows at most n such factors.

The two shorter sides of a right triangle are 6 and 8. How long is the hypotenuse?
sol: The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle. The Pythagorean theorem says a² + b² = c².
c = √100 = 10. A length is positive, so we take the positive root.
Shortcut for next time: (3, 4, 5) is a Pythagorean triple, and these sides are 2 times as long.

questions.q: Two sides of a triangle are 10 and 14 and the angle opposite the side of length 10 is 30°. How many different triangles are possible?
sol: The height from the other vertex is h = 14 sin 30° = 7.
10 is longer than 7 but shorter than 14, so two triangles fit (the ambiguous case).
questions.w: 10 is longer than 7 but shorter than 14, so two triangles fit (the ambiguous case).

questions.q: A sprinkler waters the circle (x + 1)² + (y − 2)² = 36 (units in metres). How far does the water reach from the sprinkler (m)?
sol: A circle with centre (h, k) and radius r has the equation (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r².
Match the form: the centre is (−1, 2) (the signs in the brackets are flipped), and r² = 36.
r = √36 = 6. Radius is a distance, so it is positive. The water reaches 6 m.

questions.q: The ellipse x²/169 + y²/25 = 1 has foci at (±c, 0). Find c.
sol: The larger denominator (169) is under x², so the long direction is horizontal and the foci sit on the x-axis. That makes a² = 169 and b² = 25.
For an ellipse, c² = a² − b² = 169 − 25 = 144.
c = √144 = 12, so the foci are at (±12, 0).

questions.q: The parabola y = x²/4 has its focus at (0, p). Find p.

p = 4 ÷ 4 = 1, so the focus is at (0, 1).

a² = 25, so a = 5. Then c² = a² − b² = 25 − 16 = 9, so c = 3.

questions.q: A circle has radius 6 cm. Find the arc length for a central angle of 40° (cm, 2 decimals).
sol: Arc length is a fraction of the circumference. The fraction is 40/360.
Using radians makes it simple: s = rθ. First convert 40° × π/180 = 0.6981 rad.

questions.q: A sector of a circle with radius 6 cm has a central angle of 40°. Find its area (cm², 1 decimal).
sol: A sector is a slice of the whole circle’s area πr². The slice is 40/360 of it.
In radians the formula is A = ½ r² θ, with θ = 0.6981 rad.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, A = 30°, a = 5, b = 8. How many different triangles are possible?
sol: This is the SSA (ambiguous) case. Compare the side across from A with the height h = b sin A = 4.
Here a = 5, which is bigger than h and smaller than b = 8.
a is long enough to reach the base line but shorter than b, so it can swing to two places: 2 triangles.
questions.w: Compare a with b sin A and with b.

questions.w: Compare a with b sin A and with b.

questions.q: Two sides of a triangle are 7 and 9 with an included angle of 60°. Find the third side (2 decimals).
sol: Law of Cosines is the Pythagorean theorem with a correction for the angle: c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C.
Check: at C = 90° the extra term vanishes and we get Pythagoras. For C = 60° the side is shorter than that.

Check: at C = 90° the extra term vanishes and we get Pythagoras. For C = 75° the side is shorter than that.

questions.q: Use Heron’s formula to find the area of a triangle with sides 13, 14, 15 (2 decimals).
sol: Heron’s formula needs only the three sides. First the semi-perimeter s = (a + b + c) ÷ 2 = 21.

questions.q: Use Heron’s formula to find the area of a triangle with sides 7, 8, 9 (2 decimals).
sol: Heron’s formula needs only the three sides. First the semi-perimeter s = (a + b + c) ÷ 2 = 12.

questions.q: Use Heron’s formula to find the area of a triangle with sides 9, 10, 17 (2 decimals).
sol: Heron’s formula needs only the three sides. First the semi-perimeter s = (a + b + c) ÷ 2 = 18.

questions.q: For y = 3 sin(2(x − 1)) + -1, find the period (decimal, 3 places).
sol: For y = A sin(B(x − C)) + D, the number multiplying x inside sets how fast the wave repeats.
Normal sine takes 2π to repeat. With B = 2 it repeats 2 times as fast.
Amplitude (3), shift C (1) and midline D (-1) do not change the period.

questions.q: For y = 2 sin(4(x − )) + 5, find the period (decimal, 3 places).
sol: For y = A sin(B(x − C)) + D, the number multiplying x inside sets how fast the wave repeats.
Normal sine takes 2π to repeat. With B = 4 it repeats 4 times as fast.
Amplitude (2), shift C () and midline D (5) do not change the period.

questions.q: For y = 5 sin(3(x − 2)) + , find the period (decimal, 3 places).
sol: For y = A sin(B(x − C)) + D, the number multiplying x inside sets how fast the wave repeats.
Normal sine takes 2π to repeat. With B = 3 it repeats 3 times as fast.
Amplitude (5), shift C (2) and midline D () do not change the period.

questions.q: For y = 1.5 sin(6(x − 1)) + 2, find the period (decimal, 3 places).
sol: For y = A sin(B(x − C)) + D, the number multiplying x inside sets how fast the wave repeats.
Normal sine takes 2π to repeat. With B = 6 it repeats 6 times as fast.
Amplitude (1.5), shift C (1) and midline D (2) do not change the period.

questions.q: y = −2 cos(x) + 3 has what range?
sol: The midline is y = 3 (the +3 shifts the whole wave up).
The amplitude is |−2| = 2, so it goes 2 above and 2 below the midline: 3 − 2 = 1 to 3 + 2 = 5.
The negative sign only flips the wave upside down; it does not change the range.

questions.q: Match each function to its period.
sol: Sine and cosine: period 2π ÷ B. Tangent: period π ÷ B.
sin 2x: 2π/2 = π. cos(x/2): 2π ÷ ½ = 4π. tan(x/2): π ÷ ½ = 2π.
questions.w: Divide the base period by B.

questions.q: Put the transformations in a sensible order to sketch y = 2 sin(3x − π) + 1.
items: Read off amplitude 2, period 2π/3, phase shift π/3 right, midline y = 1
Draw the midline y = 1 and the max/min lines y = 3 and y = −1
Start one cycle at x = π/3 and mark five key points a quarter-period apart
sol: Factor the 3 out of the argument to see the true horizontal shift: 3x − π = 3(x − π/3).
Each piece (A, B, C, D) controls one visible feature.
questions.w: Factor first, then read A, B, C, D, then plot.

questions.q: Find the remainder when x³ − 4x² − 7x + 10 is divided by (x − 2).
sol: Remainder Theorem: dividing p(x) by (x − k) leaves remainder p(k). Why? p(x) = (x − k)q(x) + r, and plugging in x = k kills the first term.

questions.q: Find the remainder when 2x³ + 3x² − 5x + 6 is divided by (x + 1).
sol: Remainder Theorem: dividing p(x) by (x − k) leaves remainder p(k). Why? p(x) = (x − k)q(x) + r, and plugging in x = k kills the first term.

questions.q: Find the remainder when x³ + 0x² − 3x + 5 is divided by (x − 3).
sol: Remainder Theorem: dividing p(x) by (x − k) leaves remainder p(k). Why? p(x) = (x − k)q(x) + r, and plugging in x = k kills the first term.

questions.q: Find the remainder when 3x³ − 2x² + 0x − 8 is divided by (x − 2).
sol: Remainder Theorem: dividing p(x) by (x − k) leaves remainder p(k). Why? p(x) = (x − k)q(x) + r, and plugging in x = k kills the first term.

questions.q: The quadratic x² + bx + c has roots 2 and 5. Find b + c.
sol: Vieta’s relations: for x² + bx + c with roots r and s, r + s = −b and rs = c.
Sum = 7, so b = -7. Product = 10, so c = 10.

questions.q: The quadratic x² + bx + c has roots -1 and 6. Find b + c.
sol: Vieta’s relations: for x² + bx + c with roots r and s, r + s = −b and rs = c.
Sum = 5, so b = -5. Product = -6, so c = -6.

questions.q: The quadratic x² + bx + c has roots 3 and 4. Find b + c.
sol: Vieta’s relations: for x² + bx + c with roots r and s, r + s = −b and rs = c.
Sum = 7, so b = -7. Product = 12, so c = 12.

questions.q: The quadratic x² + bx + c has roots -2 and -5. Find b + c.
sol: Vieta’s relations: for x² + bx + c with roots r and s, r + s = −b and rs = c.
Sum = -7, so b = 7. Product = 10, so c = 10.

questions.q: Which could be a rational root of 2x³ − 5x² + x + 6 = 0, by the Rational Root Theorem?
sol: Rational Root Theorem: any rational root p/q has p dividing the constant term (6) and q dividing the leading coefficient (2).
3/2 qualifies (3 divides 6, 2 divides 2). 5/2 fails (5 ∤ 6), 4 fails (4 ∤ 6), 1/3 fails (3 ∤ 2).

questions.q: What is the horizontal asymptote of f(x) = (3x² + 1) ÷ (x² − 4)?
sol: When the top and bottom have the same degree, the ratio of leading coefficients sets the horizontal asymptote.
Far from the origin the +1 and −4 barely matter, so f(x) ≈ 3x² ÷ x² = 3.
y = 3 (x = 2 is a vertical asymptote, not a horizontal one).

questions.q: What happens to f(x) = (x² − 9) ÷ (x − 3) at x = 3?
sol: The (x − 3) cancels, so f(x) = x + 3 everywhere except x = 3, where the original is undefined.
Cancelled factor = hole, at height 3 + 3 = 6. A factor that stays in the denominator would be an asymptote.

questions.q: $1000 is invested at 5% compounded continuously. How much is it worth after 10 years? ($, 2 decimals)
sol: Continuous compounding is the limit of compounding more and more often: A = P e^(rt).

questions.q: $2500 is invested at 4% compounded continuously. How much is it worth after 15 years? ($, 2 decimals)

questions.q: Solve 2^x = 50 (decimal, 3 places).
sol: x is the exponent, so “undo” the power with a logarithm. Taking log of both sides brings the exponent down: x log 2 = log 50.

questions.q: Solve 3^x = 100 (decimal, 3 places).
sol: x is the exponent, so “undo” the power with a logarithm. Taking log of both sides brings the exponent down: x log 3 = log 100.

questions.q: Solve 5^x = 200 (decimal, 3 places).
sol: x is the exponent, so “undo” the power with a logarithm. Taking log of both sides brings the exponent down: x log 5 = log 200.

questions.q: Which equals log₂ 40 − log₂ 5?
sol: Subtracting logs divides the numbers: log a − log b = log (a ÷ b).

questions.q: Why must you check solutions after solving log₃(x) + log₃(x − 8) = 2?
o: Combining logs can introduce an x that makes a log argument negative
Equations with logs have no solutions
sol: x = −1 makes log₃(−1) undefined. Only x = 9 works. Always test the domain (arguments must be positive).
questions.w: Extraneous solutions come from the domain.

questions.q: Multiply (2 + 3i)(1 − 4i). What is the real part?
sol: Treat i like a variable and expand, remembering i² = −1 (the rule that makes complex numbers work).
The i² term becomes 12, so the real part is 2 + 12 = 14.

questions.q: Multiply (3 − 1i)(2 + 5i). What is the real part?
sol: Treat i like a variable and expand, remembering i² = −1 (the rule that makes complex numbers work).
The i² term becomes 5, so the real part is 6 + 5 = 11.

questions.q: Multiply (4 + 2i)(-1 + 3i). What is the real part?
sol: Treat i like a variable and expand, remembering i² = −1 (the rule that makes complex numbers work).
The i² term becomes -6, so the real part is -4 + -6 = -10.

questions.q: The discriminant of 2x² − 4x + 5 is negative. What does that tell you?
o: Two non-real complex solutions that are conjugates
sol: The discriminant b² − 4ac is what sits under the square root in the quadratic formula.
Here (−4)² − 4(2)(5) = 16 − 40 = −24, and the square root of a negative number is imaginary.
So x = (4 ± i√24) ÷ 4, a conjugate pair. The graph never touches the x-axis.
questions.w: Negative discriminant means complex conjugate roots.

questions.q: An arithmetic sequence has first term 5 and common difference 3. Find the sum of the first 20 terms.
sol: Gauss’s trick: pair the first and last terms, the second and second-last, and so on. Every pair has the same sum.
Number of pairs is n/2, each summing to a₁ + aₙ = 67: S = 20/2 × (5 + 62).

questions.q: An arithmetic sequence has first term -2 and common difference 4. Find the sum of the first 15 terms.
sol: Gauss’s trick: pair the first and last terms, the second and second-last, and so on. Every pair has the same sum.
Number of pairs is n/2, each summing to a₁ + aₙ = 52: S = 15/2 × (-2 + 54).

questions.q: An arithmetic sequence has first term 10 and common difference -2. Find the sum of the first 12 terms.
sol: Gauss’s trick: pair the first and last terms, the second and second-last, and so on. Every pair has the same sum.
Number of pairs is n/2, each summing to a₁ + aₙ = -2: S = 12/2 × (10 + -12).

questions.q: Find the sum of the infinite geometric series 81 + 27 + 9 + … (decimal).
sol: An infinite sum can be finite when each term shrinks. It works only if |r| < 1; here r = 0.3333.
Formula: S = a₁ ÷ (1 − r). It comes from S − rS = a₁, since all later terms cancel.

questions.q: Find the sum of the infinite geometric series 12 + 6 + 3 + … (decimal).
sol: An infinite sum can be finite when each term shrinks. It works only if |r| < 1; here r = 0.5.
Formula: S = a₁ ÷ (1 − r). It comes from S − rS = a₁, since all later terms cancel.

questions.q: Find the sum of the infinite geometric series 5 + 1 + 0.2 + … (decimal).
sol: An infinite sum can be finite when each term shrinks. It works only if |r| < 1; here r = 0.2.
Formula: S = a₁ ÷ (1 − r). It comes from S − rS = a₁, since all later terms cancel.

questions.q: The ellipse x²/25 + y²/9 = 1 has a² = 25 and b² = 9. How far is each focus from the centre? (c)
sol: In an ellipse the two foci are on the longer axis. Every point has the same total distance to both foci.
The three lengths a (semi-major), b (semi-minor), c (centre to focus) form a right triangle: c² = a² − b².

questions.q: The ellipse x²/169 + y²/25 = 1 has a² = 169 and b² = 25. How far is each focus from the centre? (c)

questions.q: Which conic is x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 3 = 0?
o: A circle with centre (3, −2) and radius 4
A circle with centre (−3, 2) and radius 4
sol: Complete the square in both variables: (x² − 6x + 9) + (y² + 4y + 4) = 3 + 9 + 4.
Standard form (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r² gives centre (3, −2) and r = 4. The signs in the equation are opposite to the centre coordinates.

questions.q: The hyperbola x²/16 − y²/9 = 1 has asymptotes with slopes:
sol: For x²/a² − y²/b² = 1, far from the origin the “1” is negligible, so x²/a² ≈ y²/b².
a² = 16 so a = 4; b² = 9 so b = 3. Slopes are ±3/4.

questions.q: Convert the polar point (r, θ) = (4, 60°) to rectangular coordinates. What is x? (decimal, 3 places)
sol: Polar describes a point by distance r and angle θ. Rectangular reads the same point as right/left (x) and up/down (y).
The right triangle gives x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ.

questions.q: Convert the polar point (r, θ) = (6, 150°) to rectangular coordinates. What is x? (decimal, 3 places)

The right triangle gives x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ.

questions.q: A particle moves with x = 2t + 1 and y = t². Find y when x = 7.
sol: Parametric equations give x and y both in terms of a third variable t (often time).
To find y at a given x, first find the t that produces that x: 2t + 1 = 7 gives t = 3.

questions.q: A particle moves with x = 3t − 1 and y = t². Find y when x = 5.

To find y at a given x, first find the t that produces that x: 4t + 2 = -2 gives t = -1.

questions.q: The inverse of f(x) = (x − 3) ÷ 2 is f⁻¹(x) = 2x + 3. What is f⁻¹(2)?
sol: An inverse undoes the function. f subtracts 3 then divides by 2, so f⁻¹ multiplies by 2 then adds 3 (reverse order, opposite operations).

questions.q: The inverse of f(x) = (x − -4) ÷ 5 is f⁻¹(x) = 5x + -4. What is f⁻¹(2)?
sol: An inverse undoes the function. f subtracts -4 then divides by 5, so f⁻¹ multiplies by 5 then adds -4 (reverse order, opposite operations).

questions.q: The inverse of f(x) = (x − 7) ÷ 3 is f⁻¹(x) = 3x + 7. What is f⁻¹(2)?
sol: An inverse undoes the function. f subtracts 7 then divides by 3, so f⁻¹ multiplies by 3 then adds 7 (reverse order, opposite operations).

questions.q: The graph of y = f(x − 3) + 2 is the graph of y = f(x) moved:
sol: Inside the brackets, x − 3 means the input is delayed: the graph needs a larger x to give the same output, so it moves right 3.
Outside, + 2 simply lifts every output by 2.
questions.w: x − 3 inside shifts right; + 2 outside shifts up.

questions.q: Which transformation of f(x) is a reflection across the y-axis?
sol: Reflecting across the y-axis swaps left and right: the point (a, b) goes to (−a, b).
That means the input sign flips: y = f(−x).
−f(x) flips the outputs instead (a reflection across the x-axis).
questions.w: Negate the input for a y-axis reflection.

questions.q: Is f(x) = x³ − x even, odd, or neither?
sol: That equals −(x³ − x) = −f(x), the definition of an odd function.
Its graph has rotational symmetry about the origin.

questions.q: Select ALL functions that are one-to-one (have an inverse function) on all real numbers.
sol: A one-to-one function passes the horizontal line test: no output is repeated.
Lines with nonzero slope, x³ and 2ˣ always rise, so they pass.
x² and |x| give the same output for x and −x, so they fail on all real numbers.

questions.q: The parabola y = 2(x − 3)² − 5 has its vertex at (h, k). Find h + k.
sol: Vertex form y = a(x − h)² + k shows the turning point directly: (h, k).
h is the number that makes the bracket zero. Here x − 3 = 0 gives h = 3.
k is the added constant, -5. h + k = -2.

questions.q: The parabola y = −(x − 4)² + 7 has its vertex at (h, k). Find h + k.
sol: Vertex form y = a(x − h)² + k shows the turning point directly: (h, k).
h is the number that makes the bracket zero. Here x − 4 = 0 gives h = 4.
k is the added constant, 7. h + k = 11.

questions.q: The parabola y = 3(x + 2)² + 1 has its vertex at (h, k). Find h + k.
sol: Vertex form y = a(x − h)² + k shows the turning point directly: (h, k).
h is the number that makes the bracket zero. Here x + 2 = 0 gives h = -2.
k is the added constant, 1. h + k = -1.

questions.q: The parabola y = (x − 5)² − 9 has its vertex at (h, k). Find h + k.
sol: Vertex form y = a(x − h)² + k shows the turning point directly: (h, k).
h is the number that makes the bracket zero. Here x − 5 = 0 gives h = 5.
k is the added constant, -9. h + k = -4.

questions.q: What is (2 + 3i)(2 − 3i)?
sol: A number times its conjugate is a difference of squares: (a + bi)(a − bi) = a² − (bi)².
(bi)² = b²i² = −b², so the product is a² + b².
4 + 9 = 13. A conjugate product is always real, which is why we use it to clear i from a denominator.

questions.q: If x² + 6x + 13 = 0, what are the solutions?
sol: Alternative: complete the square: (x + 3)² = −4, so x + 3 = ±2i.

questions.q: When p(x) = x³ + 2x² − 7x + 6 is divided by (x + 1), what is the remainder?
sol: Remainder Theorem with x + 1 = x − (−1), so k = −1.

questions.q: When p(x) = x³ + 1x² − 7x + 6 is divided by (x + 1), what is the remainder?

questions.q: When p(x) = x³ + 3x² − 7x + 6 is divided by (x + 1), what is the remainder?

questions.q: A polynomial of degree 5 with real coefficients has 3 real roots (counted with multiplicity). How many non-real roots does it have?
sol: The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra: a degree-5 polynomial has exactly 5 roots counting multiplicity, real and complex.
Non-real roots of real polynomials come in conjugate pairs, so 2 is consistent (1 or 3 would not be).

questions.q: What is the end behaviour of f(x) = −2x⁴ + x³ − 5?
o: Falls to the left and falls to the right
Rises to the left and rises to the right
Falls to the left and rises to the right
Rises to the left and falls to the right
sol: For large |x| the highest-degree term dominates: −2x⁴.
Even degree: both ends point the same way. Negative leading coefficient: they point down.
So the graph falls on both sides.

questions.q: Select ALL that are factors of x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6.
sol: Test candidates with the Factor Theorem: (x − k) is a factor when p(k) = 0.
p(−1) = −24 and p(6) = 60, so those are not factors. The polynomial is (x − 1)(x − 2)(x − 3).

questions.q: Solve 6/x = x − 1 for the positive solution.
sol: Multiply both sides by x to clear the fraction: 6 = x² − x.
Rearrange: x² − x − 6 = 0, which factors as (x − 3)(x + 2) = 0.
x = 3 or x = −2. The positive solution is 3.

questions.q: After solving (x + 2)/(x − 3) = 5/(x − 3) + 1, why must you check your answer in the original equation?
o: x = 3 would make a denominator zero, so it may be extraneous
Rational equations always have two answers
You must check that it is positive
sol: Multiply by (x − 3): x + 2 = 5 + (x − 3), so x + 2 = x + 2.
That is true for every x, so the only possible failures are values excluded from the original: x = 3.
The solution is all real numbers except 3. Always list the excluded values first.
questions.w: Excluded values come from the denominators.

questions.q: What is the domain of f(x) = (x + 1)/(x² − 4)?
o: All real numbers except x = 2 and x = −2
sol: A fraction is undefined when its denominator is zero.
The numerator being zero (x = −1) is fine: that just makes the value 0.

sol: Half-life is the time for half the sample to decay, so each half-life multiplies the amount by ½.

questions.q: Which expression equals log₅ 12 using the change-of-base formula?
sol: Change of base: log_b(x) = ln x ÷ ln b. It lets a calculator with only ln or log compute any base.
questions.w: log_b x = ln x ÷ ln b.

questions.q: Solve log₂(x + 3) + log₂(x − 3) = 4 for x.
sol: Domain: x − 3 > 0 means x > 3, so x = −5 is extraneous. Answer 5.

questions.q: A population grows 8% each year. Which function gives P after t years from 500?
sol: Each year multiplies by 1 + 0.08 = 1.08 (keep 100% and add 8%).
After t years you have multiplied t times: 500 × 1.08 × 1.08 × …
Linear growth would add a fixed amount; exponential growth multiplies.

questions.q: Find the sum of the first 8 terms of the geometric sequence starting 3, 6, 12, …
sol: A geometric sum has a neat trick: S − rS leaves only the first and last terms.
S = a₁(rⁿ − 1) ÷ (r − 1) with a₁ = 3, r = 2, n = 8.

questions.q: Which angle is coterminal with −π/3?
sol: Coterminal angles differ by a full turn (2π).
They end at the same point on the unit circle.

questions.q: Convert 120° to radians (decimal, 3 places).
sol: A full turn is 360° = 2π radians, so 180° = π radians.

questions.q: Convert 210° to radians (decimal, 3 places).
sol: A full turn is 360° = 2π radians, so 180° = π radians.

questions.q: Convert 300° to radians (decimal, 3 places).
sol: A full turn is 360° = 2π radians, so 180° = π radians.

questions.q: Which equation has amplitude 3, period π and midline y = −1?
sol: Amplitude is the number in front: 3.
Midline is the constant added: −1. So y = 3 sin 2x − 1.

questions.q: Select ALL statements true for y = cos x.
sol: cos(−x) = cos x, so it is even and symmetric about the y-axis.
One full cycle is 2π and the output stays between −1 and 1.
cos 0 = 1, so the graph starts at the top, not at the origin.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, A = 40°, B = 65° and side a = 8. Find side b (2 decimals).
sol: Law of Sines: each side divided by the sine of its opposite angle is the same: a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B.
b = a sin B ÷ sin A = 8 × sin 65° ÷ sin 40°.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, A = 35°, B = 80° and side a = 12. Find side b (2 decimals).
sol: Law of Sines: each side divided by the sine of its opposite angle is the same: a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B.
b = a sin B ÷ sin A = 12 × sin 80° ÷ sin 35°.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, A = 50°, B = 60° and side a = 10. Find side b (2 decimals).
sol: Law of Sines: each side divided by the sine of its opposite angle is the same: a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B.
b = a sin B ÷ sin A = 10 × sin 60° ÷ sin 50°.

questions.q: Which law do you use first when given two sides and the angle between them (SAS)?
sol: Law of Sines needs a side and its opposite angle as a known pair. SAS has no such pair yet.
Law of Cosines uses exactly two sides and the included angle to find the third side.
After that, the Law of Sines is easy for the remaining angles.
questions.w: SAS starts with Law of Cosines.

questions.q: A circle has equation (x − 2)² + (y + 3)² = 25. What is its radius?
sol: Standard form: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r². The right-hand side is r squared, not r.

questions.q: A circle has equation (x + 4)² + (y − 1)² = 9. What is its radius?
sol: Standard form: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r². The right-hand side is r squared, not r.

questions.q: A circle has equation (x − 0)² + (y − 6)² = 49. What is its radius?
sol: Standard form: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r². The right-hand side is r squared, not r.

questions.q: A parabola has focus (0, 3) and directrix y = −3. What is its equation?
sol: Every point on a parabola is equally far from the focus and the directrix.
The vertex is halfway between them: (0, 0), with p = 3 (distance vertex to focus).

questions.q: Which conic has the equation 9x² + 4y² = 36?
sol: Both squared terms are positive with different denominators, so it is an ellipse.
If the denominators were equal it would be a circle; with a minus sign it would be a hyperbola.

questions.q: Convert the rectangular point (3, 4) to polar form. What is r?
sol: Polar r is the straight-line distance from the origin: r = √(x² + y²).

questions.q: Convert the rectangular point (5, 12) to polar form. What is r?
sol: Polar r is the straight-line distance from the origin: r = √(x² + y²).

questions.q: Convert the rectangular point (-6, 8) to polar form. What is r?
sol: Polar r is the straight-line distance from the origin: r = √(x² + y²).

questions.q: Which parametric equations trace the unit circle once as t goes from 0 to 2π?
o: x = cos t, y = sin t
x = 2 cos t, y = 2 sin t
sol: A point on the unit circle satisfies x² + y² = 1.
cos²t + sin²t = 1, so (cos t, sin t) is always on the circle and sweeps once as t covers 2π.
2 cos t and 2 sin t gives a circle of radius 2; cos 2t with sin t is not a circle.

If the bases match, set the exponents equal. Otherwise take a logarithm of both sides.
lg: log₂ 8 asks: what power of 2 gives 8? The answer is 3 because 2³ = 8. A log is an exponent in disguise.
log without a base means base 10. log 1000 = 3. Each +1 means ten times bigger.
log_b 1 = 0 and log_b b = 1, for any base.
log(ab) = log a + log b and log(a/b) = log a − log b. Logs turn multiplying into adding.
log(aⁿ) = n·log a. This is how logs pull exponents down so you can solve for them.
log_b x = log x / log b. It lets a calculator find any log.
Combine logs into one, rewrite as an exponent, solve, then check that every log's input is positive.
ln is the log with base e ≈ 2.718. ln(eˣ) = x and e^(ln x) = x.
sq: A sequence is an ordered list that follows a rule, like 3, 6, 9, 12, … Each number is a term.
You add the same amount (the common difference d) each time. The nth term is aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d.
You multiply by the same number (the common ratio r) each time. aₙ = a₁·rⁿ⁻¹.
Adding the terms: Sₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2. Gauss found 1 + 2 + … + 100 = 5050 by pairing ends.
Sₙ = a₁(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r). Each term is r times the last.
If |r| < 1 the terms shrink and the total settles on S = a₁/(1 − r). If |r| ≥ 1 it never settles.
Σ means add. Σ from k = 1 to 4 of 2k means 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 20.
Recursive: each term from the one before (aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 3). Explicit: each term from its position (aₙ = 3n + 1).
tc: A full turn is 360°. Half a turn is 180°, a quarter turn is 90°. The three angles of any triangle always add to 180°.
The sides of a right triangle
In a right triangle the longest side, across from the right angle, is the hypotenuse. For an angle you pick, the other two sides are the opposite and the adjacent.
SOH-CAH-TOA: sin = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tan = opposite ÷ adjacent. They are ratios, so they do not depend on how big the triangle is.
To find a side, write the ratio that has it and solve. To find an angle, use the inverse button: sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹.
One radian is the angle that cuts off an arc as long as the radius. A half-turn is π radians, so 180° = π rad.
On a circle of radius 1, the point at angle θ is (cos θ, sin θ). So cosine is the x-coordinate and sine is the y-coordinate.
30°, 45° and 60° have exact values: sin 30° = ½, sin 45° = √2/2, sin 60° = √3/2. Cosine reads the same list backwards.
Any angle has a reference angle (the acute angle to the x-axis). Find its value, then use the quadrant to choose + or −: All Students Take Calculus (all, sine, tangent, cosine).
tg: Sound, light, tides and alternating current all repeat in smooth waves. Sine and cosine are the mathematical models for these waves.
y = sin x starts at 0, rises to 1 at 90°, returns to 0 at 180°, falls to −1 at 270°, and repeats every 360°.
The amplitude is the distance from the midline to a peak. In y = a·sin x it is |a|.
The period is the length of one full wave. For y = sin(bx), the period is 360°/b (or 2π/b in radians). A bigger b squeezes the wave.
In y = sin(x − c) the wave slides right by c. A minus sign inside means right, plus means left.
In y = sin x + d the whole wave moves up by d. The midline is y = d. Maximum = d + |a| and minimum = d − |a|.
y = 2 sin x + 1: ranges from −1 to 3
Cosine is sine shifted left by 90°. Tangent repeats every 180° and has vertical asymptotes where cosine is 0.
To model a wave: find the midline (average of max and min), the amplitude (half the difference), and the period. Then choose sine or cosine and a shift.
tl: Many real triangles have no right angle. The Law of Sines and Law of Cosines work for every triangle.
a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use it when you know an angle and its opposite side.
c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C. It is the Pythagorean theorem with a correction term. If C = 90° the correction vanishes.
Given two sides and an angle not between them, there may be 0, 1 or 2 triangles. Check whether the side opposite the angle can reach the base.
Area = ½ab sin C. It works for any two sides and the angle between them.
A vector has a size (magnitude) and a direction. Write it as components (x, y). Its magnitude is √(x² + y²).
Add components: (a, b) + (c, d) = (a + c, b + d). A plane's ground velocity is its air velocity plus the wind's.
a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ = |a||b| cos θ. If the dot product is 0 the vectors are perpendicular.
cn: The distance between two points is a Pythagorean theorem in disguise: √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). The midpoint averages the coordinates.
A circle is every point the same distance r from a center (h, k): (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r².
A parabola is every point equally far from a point (the focus) and a line (the directrix). y = ax² has its focus at (0, 1/(4a)).
An ellipse is a stretched circle: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1. The two foci are c units from the center where c² = a² − b² (a is the longer half-axis).
A hyperbola has two branches: x²/a² − y²/b² = 1. The foci satisfy c² = a² + b² and the asymptotes are y = ±(b/a)x.
e = c/a measures how stretched a conic is. Circle e = 0, ellipse 0 < e < 1, parabola e = 1, hyperbola e > 1.
Look at the squared terms. Same sign and same coefficient: circle. Same sign, different coefficients: ellipse. Opposite signs: hyperbola. Only one squared variable: parabola.
Planets move in ellipses, satellite dishes are parabolas, and whispering galleries use ellipses to carry sound between the foci.
pp: Two ways to name a point
Rectangular coordinates give (x, y). Polar coordinates give (r, θ): how far from the origin and at what angle.
x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ.
r = √(x² + y²) and tan θ = y/x (check the quadrant).
r = 2 is a circle. r = θ spirals outward. Roses, cardioids and limaçons come from r = a cos(nθ) and similar rules.
Write x and y as functions of a third variable t, like time. They describe motion along a path.
Solve one equation for t and substitute into the other to get a relation between x and y.
Plot a + bi at (a, b). Its modulus is √(a² + b²) and its argument is the angle from the real axis.
In polar form, multiplying complex numbers multiplies the moduli and adds the angles. So (r cis θ)ⁿ = rⁿ cis(nθ).

cards.t: After one half-life, half remains. After two, a quarter. Amount = start × (½)^(time ÷ half-life).

lab.hook: After each half-life, half is left.
lab.out: Half-life = {h}. After {h} steps there is 50%; after {=2*h|0}, 25%.

cards.t: If the bases match, set the exponents equal. Otherwise take a logarithm of both sides.

lessons.title: What a logarithm asks · Common logs

cards.t: log₂ 8 asks: what power of 2 gives 8? The answer is 3 because 2³ = 8. A log is an exponent in disguise.

lab.hook: A log asks: what power do I need?

cards.t: log without a base means base 10. log 1000 = 3. Each +1 means ten times bigger.
log_b 1 = 0 and log_b b = 1, for any base.

lessons.title: Product and quotient rules · Power rule

cards.t: log(ab) = log a + log b and log(a/b) = log a − log b. Logs turn multiplying into adding.

lab.hook: Logs turn multiplying into adding.
lab.note: If A = 10^{a} and B = 10^{b}, then A×B = 10^{=a+b|0}. Multiply → add the exponents.

cards.t: log(aⁿ) = n·log a. This is how logs pull exponents down so you can solve for them.
log_b x = log x / log b. It lets a calculator find any log.

lessons.title: Solving log equations · Natural log

cards.t: Combine logs into one, rewrite as an exponent, solve, then check that every log's input is positive.
ln is the log with base e ≈ 2.718. ln(eˣ) = x and e^(ln x) = x.

lessons.title: Patterns and sequences · Arithmetic sequences

cards.t: A sequence is an ordered list that follows a rule, like 3, 6, 9, 12, … Each number is a term.

lab.hook: A sequence is a list that follows a rule.

cards.t: You add the same amount (the common difference d) each time. The nth term is aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d.

lab.hook: Each term adds the same amount d.

cards.t: You multiply by the same number (the common ratio r) each time. aₙ = a₁·rⁿ⁻¹.

lab.hook: Each term multiplies by the same ratio r.

lessons.title: Arithmetic series · Geometric series

cards.t: Adding the terms: Sₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2. Gauss found 1 + 2 + … + 100 = 5050 by pairing ends.
Sₙ = a₁(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r). Each term is r times the last.
If |r| < 1 the terms shrink and the total settles on S = a₁/(1 − r). If |r| ≥ 1 it never settles.

lessons.title: Sigma notation · Recursive and explicit rules

cards.t: Σ means add. Σ from k = 1 to 4 of 2k means 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 20.
Recursive: each term from the one before (aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 3). Explicit: each term from its position (aₙ = 3n + 1).

lessons.title: Turns and degrees · The sides of a right triangle

cards.t: A full turn is 360°. Half a turn is 180°, a quarter turn is 90°. The three angles of any triangle always add to 180°.

cards.h: The sides of a right triangle
cards.t: In a right triangle the longest side, across from the right angle, is the hypotenuse. For an angle you pick, the other two sides are the opposite and the adjacent.
SOH-CAH-TOA: sin = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tan = opposite ÷ adjacent. They are ratios, so they do not depend on how big the triangle is.

lab.hook: Slide the angle and the size. Watch the ratios.
lab.take: sin = opp/hyp, cos = adj/hyp, tan = opp/adj. The ratios depend only on the angle.

lessons.title: Finding sides and angles · Radians

cards.t: To find a side, write the ratio that has it and solve. To find an angle, use the inverse button: sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹.
One radian is the angle that cuts off an arc as long as the radius. A half-turn is π radians, so 180° = π rad.

lab.hook: A radian is an angle measured by arc length.
lab.note: {d}° = {=d*pi/180|3} radians. A half turn (180°) is π ≈ 3.14.

cards.t: On a circle of radius 1, the point at angle θ is (cos θ, sin θ). So cosine is the x-coordinate and sine is the y-coordinate.

lab.hook: Drag the angle around the circle. Read sin and cos from the point.

pre.q: At 90°, the point is straight up. What is cos 90°?
pre.why: The point is (0, 1): x = cos = 0, y = sin = 1.

lab.take: On the unit circle, the point is (cos θ, sin θ).

lessons.title: Special angles · Reference angles and signs

cards.t: 30°, 45° and 60° have exact values: sin 30° = ½, sin 45° = √2/2, sin 60° = √3/2. Cosine reads the same list backwards.

lab.hook: Set the angle to 30°, 45°, 60°. Notice the values.

cards.t: Any angle has a reference angle (the acute angle to the x-axis). Find its value, then use the quadrant to choose + or −: All Students Take Calculus (all, sine, tangent, cosine).

lab.hook: Move through the four quadrants. When are sin and cos negative?

pre.q: In quadrant II (90°–180°), which is negative?
pre.why: x is negative there, so cos is negative while sin stays positive.

lessons.title: Waves in everyday life · The sine graph

cards.t: Sound, light, tides and alternating current all repeat in smooth waves. Sine and cosine are the mathematical models for these waves.
y = sin x starts at 0, rises to 1 at 90°, returns to 0 at 180°, falls to −1 at 270°, and repeats every 360°.

lab.hook: Trace the unit circle height as the angle grows.
lab.out: One full wave every 360°.

cards.t: The amplitude is the distance from the midline to a peak. In y = a·sin x it is |a|.

lab.hook: Amplitude is how tall the wave is from the middle.
lab.out: Amplitude = {A}: the wave goes up to {A} and down to −{A}.

lessons.title: Period · Phase shift

cards.t: The period is the length of one full wave. For y = sin(bx), the period is 360°/b (or 2π/b in radians). A bigger b squeezes the wave.

lab.hook: Period is how long one full wave takes.

cards.t: In y = sin(x − c) the wave slides right by c. A minus sign inside means right, plus means left.

lab.hook: Phase shift slides the wave left or right.
lab.out: Blue is shifted right by {c}°. Gold is the original.

cards.t: In y = sin x + d the whole wave moves up by d. The midline is y = d. Maximum = d + |a| and minimum = d − |a|.
cards.f: y = 2 sin x + 1: ranges from −1 to 3

lab.hook: Vertical shift moves the middle line up or down.
lab.out: Middle line at y = {k}.

lessons.title: Cosine and tangent graphs · Modeling with sinusoids

cards.t: Cosine is sine shifted left by 90°. Tangent repeats every 180° and has vertical asymptotes where cosine is 0.

lab.hook: Cosine is sine shifted. Tangent has asymptotes.
lab.out: Cosine (blue) is sine (gold) shifted 90° left.

cards.t: To model a wave: find the midline (average of max and min), the amplitude (half the difference), and the period. Then choose sine or cosine and a shift.

lab.hook: A Ferris wheel height is a wave: height = r·sin + middle.
lab.out: One turn every {T} minutes. Height swings from 1 m to 15 m.

lessons.title: Triangles that are not right · Law of Sines

cards.t: Many real triangles have no right angle. The Law of Sines and Law of Cosines work for every triangle.
a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use it when you know an angle and its opposite side.

lab.hook: In every triangle, side ÷ sin(opposite angle) is the same.
lab.eq: a / sin A = b / sin B

cards.t: c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C. It is the Pythagorean theorem with a correction term. If C = 90° the correction vanishes.

lessons.title: The ambiguous case (SSA) · Area with sine

cards.t: Given two sides and an angle not between them, there may be 0, 1 or 2 triangles. Check whether the side opposite the angle can reach the base.
Area = ½ab sin C. It works for any two sides and the angle between them.
A vector has a size (magnitude) and a direction. Write it as components (x, y). Its magnitude is √(x² + y²).

lessons.title: Adding vectors · Dot product and angles

cards.t: Add components: (a, b) + (c, d) = (a + c, b + d). A plane's ground velocity is its air velocity plus the wind's.
a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ = |a||b| cos θ. If the dot product is 0 the vectors are perpendicular.

lessons.title: Distance and midpoint · Circles

cards.t: The distance between two points is a Pythagorean theorem in disguise: √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). The midpoint averages the coordinates.

dd.why: Draw a right triangle with the two points as the ends of the long slanted side. Its horizontal leg has length |x2 - x1| and its vertical leg has length |y2 - y1|. The Pythagorean theorem then says distance^2 = (x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2, so the distance is the square root. The differences are squared, so it does not matter which point you call first. The midpoint is the halfway spot, and halfway in x is the average of the two x values, same for y.
dd.pic: Plot (1, 2) and (7, 10) on graph paper. Draw a horizontal line from (1, 2) to (7, 2), then a vertical line up to (7, 10). Those two lines and the slanted segment form your right triangle. Mark the middle of the slanted segment: that is the midpoint.
dd.analogy: Walking diagonally across a city grid: the blocks east and north are the legs, and the straight-line shortcut is the hypotenuse. The analogy stops working because real streets force you to walk the legs, while distance measures the straight shortcut.
ways: Distance: how far east/west, how far north/south, then the diagonal. Midpoint: add the two x values and halve, add the two y values and halve.
(1, 2) to (7, 10): legs are 6 and 8, so distance = sqrt(36 + 64) = 10. Midpoint = (8/2, 12/2) = (4, 6).
If the legs are a Pythagorean triple (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 6-8-10), the distance is a whole number. Spot those to skip the calculator.

ex.q: Find the distance between (1, 2) and (7, 10) and the midpoint.
steps: Square both and add: 36 + 64 = 100, because the legs of a right triangle give the hypotenuse squared.
Average the y values: (2 + 10)/2 = 6, so the midpoint is (4, 6).

dd.trap: Forgetting the square root and giving 100 as the distance, or writing x2 - x1 but y1 - y2 and mixing up signs. Squaring fixes the sign, but you must take the root at the end.
dd.tip: Distance is Pythagoras wearing a coordinate costume; midpoint is the average of the two ends.

cards.t: A circle is every point the same distance r from a center (h, k): (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r².

lab.hook: A circle is every point at the same distance r from the center.

dd.why: A circle is defined by one rule: every point is exactly r from the center (h, k). The distance formula says the distance from (x, y) to (h, k) is sqrt((x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2). Setting that equal to r and squaring both sides removes the root and gives (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2. The h and k have minus signs because the equation measures how far x is from h. If the center were different, the same shape just slides, which is why h and k are shifts. The right side is r squared, not r, so the radius is the square root of that number.
dd.pic: Draw a dot at the center (h, k). Use a compass to draw a circle of radius r around it. Pick any point on the circle, drop a vertical line and a horizontal line from it to the center's height and column: you get a right triangle with hypotenuse r.
dd.analogy: A sprinkler that throws water exactly r meters in every direction wets a circle. The sprinkler is the center and the wet edge is the equation. It stops working as a model once the water is thrown unevenly, which breaks the equal-distance rule.
ways: All points exactly r from the center.
(x - 2)^2 + (y + 1)^2 = 9 has center (2, -1) and radius 3. The point (5, -1) fits: 3^2 + 0 = 9.
Flip the sign inside the parentheses to get the center; take the square root of the right side to get the radius.

ex.q: Find the center and radius of (x + 3)^2 + (y + 1)^2 = 25, and say whether (1, 2) is on the circle.
steps: Write x + 3 as x - (-3): the center x is -3.
Write y + 1 as y - (-1): the center y is -1, so the center is (-3, -1).
The right side is r^2 = 25, so r = 5.
It equals 25, so (1, 2) is exactly 5 units from the center and is on the circle.

dd.trap: Reading the center with the wrong sign, such as calling (x + 3) a center of +3, or using 25 as the radius. Remember the center is the opposite sign, the radius is the square root.
dd.tip: Inside the bracket, the sign lies; the center is the opposite.

cards.t: A parabola is every point equally far from a point (the focus) and a line (the directrix). y = ax² has its focus at (0, 1/(4a)).

lab.hook: A parabola opens toward its focus.
lab.out: y = x²/(4·{p}). The focus is {p} above the vertex.

dd.why: A parabola is the set of points that are the same distance from a fixed point (focus) and a fixed line (directrix). For y = ax^2 put the focus at (0, p) and the directrix at y = -p. A point (x, y) is equally far from both when sqrt(x^2 + (y - p)^2) = y + p. Square both sides: x^2 + y^2 - 2py + p^2 = y^2 + 2py + p^2, which leaves x^2 = 4py. So y = x^2/(4p), meaning a = 1/(4p) and p = 1/(4a). A big a is a narrow parabola with the focus close to the vertex.
dd.pic: Draw an x-axis and a dot at (0, 1) as the focus. Draw the horizontal line y = -1 as the directrix. Mark the vertex halfway between them at the origin. Pick a point on the curve and draw two segments of equal length: one straight down to the directrix and one to the focus.
dd.analogy: A satellite dish: signals arrive in parallel and bounce to the single focus point. The analogy to equal distances is loose here; the real reason is that the shape is built so every bounced path to the focus has the same total length.
ways: Equidistant from a point and a line; the vertex sits halfway between them.
y = x^2/4: a = 1/4, so p = 1/(4 x 1/4) = 1. Focus (0, 1), directrix y = -1. The point (2, 1) is on the curve and is 2 from the focus and 2 from the line.
Write the parabola as x^2 = 4py; the number in front of y is 4p.

ex.q: Find the focus of y = x^2/8.
steps: Match y = x^2/8 to y = x^2/(4p): 4p = 8.
The vertex is at the origin and the parabola opens up, so the focus is p above it.
The focus is (0, 2); the directrix is y = -2.
Check with the point (4, 2): its distance to the focus (0, 2) is 4 and to the line y = -2 is 4. They match.

dd.trap: Saying p = 1/a or using the number in the denominator directly. The denominator is 4p, so you must divide by 4.
dd.tip: x squared equals four p y: four p is the number under the y.

lessons.title: Ellipses · Hyperbolas

cards.t: An ellipse is a stretched circle: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1. The two foci are c units from the center where c² = a² − b² (a is the longer half-axis).

dd.why: An ellipse is every point whose distances to two foci add up to the same constant, 2a. At the end of the short axis, the point is a from each focus by symmetry, so the right triangle with legs b and c and hypotenuse a gives a^2 = b^2 + c^2. That is why c^2 = a^2 - b^2. If a = b, c = 0 and the foci merge into the center, giving a circle. The longer axis is the one under the bigger denominator, and the foci sit on that axis.
dd.pic: Draw an x-axis and y-axis. Mark points (5, 0), (-5, 0), (0, 3), (0, -3) and sketch a smooth oval through them. Put dots at (4, 0) and (-4, 0): those are the foci. Draw a string from each focus to a point on the oval.
dd.analogy: Two friends hold a loop of string around two pins and pull it tight with a pencil: the pencil traces an ellipse. The pins are the foci. It stops working if the string is shorter than the gap between the pins, because then no ellipse exists.
ways: Sum of distances to two foci is constant; c is the focus distance from the center.
Bigger denominator minus smaller denominator, then square root, gives c.

ex.q: Find the foci of x^2/169 + y^2/25 = 1.
steps: Find the larger denominator: 169, so a = 13 along the x-axis.
Check: the point (0, 5) has distance sqrt(144 + 25) = 13 to each focus, and 13 + 13 = 26 = 2a.

dd.trap: Using a^2 + b^2 (the hyperbola rule) for an ellipse, or placing the foci on the wrong axis. For an ellipse c is always smaller than a.
dd.tip: Ellipse: subtract, stay inside (c < a). Hyperbola: add, go outside.

cards.t: A hyperbola has two branches: x²/a² − y²/b² = 1. The foci satisfy c² = a² + b² and the asymptotes are y = ±(b/a)x.

dd.why: A hyperbola is every point where the difference of the distances to two foci is constant. Far from the center, the +1 on the right of x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1 matters less and less, so the curve nearly satisfies x^2/a^2 = y^2/b^2. That means y = +/-(b/a)x, and those lines are the asymptotes the branches hug. The foci satisfy c^2 = a^2 + b^2 because the two distances differ by 2a and the geometry adds the squares. Since c is bigger than a, the foci sit outside the vertices.
dd.pic: Draw a box centered at the origin that reaches x = +/-a and y = +/-b. Draw the two diagonals of the box and extend them forever: these are the asymptotes. Sketch the two branches starting at the vertices (+/-a, 0) and bending toward the diagonals without touching.
dd.analogy: Two radio towers: a ship that hears signals arriving with a fixed time gap sits on a hyperbola. The gap is the constant difference of distances. The model breaks down because real signals need a third tower to pin down a single point.
ways: Two curves that open away from each other, approaching two diagonal lines.
x^2/4 - y^2/16 = 1: a = 2, b = 4, asymptote slope b/a = 2, c = sqrt(20) = about 4.47.
The box from (-2, -4) to (2, 4); diagonals are y = 2x and y = -2x; branches open left and right.

ex.q: Find the asymptotes of x^2/9 - y^2/25 = 1 and the foci.
steps: Read a^2 = 9 so a = 3, and b^2 = 25 so b = 5.
The foci are (+/-sqrt(34), 0), because the x^2 term is positive so the branches open sideways.

dd.trap: Using the slope a/b instead of b/a, or thinking the curve crosses the asymptotes. Slope is y over x: b over a.
dd.tip: Hyperbola slope is b over a: box height over box width.

cards.t: e = c/a measures how stretched a conic is. Circle e = 0, ellipse 0 < e < 1, parabola e = 1, hyperbola e > 1.

dd.why: Eccentricity measures how far the foci sit from the center compared with the half-width a. For a circle the foci are at the center so c = 0 and e = 0. As the foci move outward the ellipse gets flatter, so e grows toward 1. A parabola is the limit with one focus gone to infinity, so e = 1. For a hyperbola c > a, so e > 1. This one number sorts every conic. If it were not a ratio, a big ellipse and a small ellipse of the same shape would look different; dividing by a removes the size.
dd.pic: Draw a number line from 0 to 3. Mark 0 as circle, put ellipses between 0 and 1, mark 1 as parabola, and put hyperbolas to the right of 1. Then sketch three ovals from nearly round to long and thin and place them along the 0 to 1 stretch.
dd.analogy: Think of how stretched a rubber band is: loose and round at e = 0, pulled tight and thin close to e = 1. The analogy fails at e = 1 and above, where the band snaps open into a curve that never closes.
ways: How far the foci are from the center compared with the half-width.
x^2/25 + y^2/9 = 1: c = 4, a = 5, e = 0.8. A much rounder ellipse with c = 1, a = 5 has e = 0.2.
e below 1 closes up, e = 1 is a parabola, e above 1 opens up.

ex.q: Find the eccentricity of x^2/25 + y^2/9 = 1 and of x^2/9 - y^2/16 = 1.

dd.trap: Dividing by b instead of a, or getting e over 1 for an ellipse. Always divide by a, the semi-major length.
dd.tip: e under 1 is closed, over 1 is open.

lessons.title: Identifying a conic · Real-world conics

cards.t: Look at the squared terms. Same sign and same coefficient: circle. Same sign, different coefficients: ellipse. Opposite signs: hyperbola. Only one squared variable: parabola.

dd.why: Conic sections come from slicing a cone, and their equations differ by the squared terms. A circle treats x and y equally, so both squares have the same positive coefficient. An ellipse stretches one direction, giving different positive coefficients. A hyperbola subtracts, so the signs are opposite. A parabola has only one squared variable because the other variable is a first power. Reading the squares first is like reading the DNA of the equation: you can classify without graphing.
dd.pic: Draw a double cone (two ice cream cones tip to tip). Slice it flat across for a circle, slightly tilted for an ellipse, parallel to the side for a parabola, and steeply through both cones for a hyperbola. Next to each, write the squared-term pattern.
dd.analogy: Think of sorting laundry by the tag: you do not need to wash it to know where it goes. The tag is the signs and coefficients of the squares. The analogy fails when there is an xy term or a rotated conic, which needs extra work.
ways: Same sign and same size: circle. Same sign, different size: ellipse. Opposite signs: hyperbola. One square only: parabola.
x^2 + y^2 = 9: circle. 4x^2 + y^2 = 36: ellipse. x^2 - y^2 = 1: hyperbola. y = x^2 - 3: parabola.
Count squares, check signs, compare sizes.

steps: First equation: both squares are positive, so it is a circle or an ellipse.
The denominators 25 and 16 differ, so it is an ellipse.
Second equation: x^2 is positive and y^2 is negative, opposite signs.
Divide by 36 to see x^2/4 - y^2/9 = 1, which confirms the hyperbola form.

dd.trap: Thinking x^2/25 + y^2/25 = 1 is an ellipse. The denominators match, so it is a circle with radius 5. Compare the sizes after dividing.
dd.tip: Same sign same size circle, same sign different size oval, different sign hyper.

cards.t: Planets move in ellipses, satellite dishes are parabolas, and whispering galleries use ellipses to carry sound between the foci.

dd.why: Each conic has a focus property that makes it useful. A parabola sends all parallel rays that hit it to the single focus, so dishes collect weak signals into one point. An ellipse has the property that any path from one focus to the curve and then to the other focus has the same length, so sound or light leaving one focus reaches the other at the same time. Planets follow ellipses because gravity pulls with an inverse-square force, and Kepler found the Sun sits at one focus. Hyperbolas appear in navigation and in the path of a fast comet that escapes.
dd.pic: Draw an ellipse with its two foci. From the left focus, draw three lines to different points on the oval, then bounce each to the right focus. Label all three paths with the same total length. Next to it, sketch a parabola with vertical arrows coming down and bouncing to the focus.
dd.analogy: A whispering gallery is like two friends standing at the pins of a string loop: a quiet word at one focus bounces off the wall and lands exactly at the other. It stops working if the room's shape is not a true ellipse.
ways: Parabola collects, ellipse links its two foci, hyperbola describes escape paths.
Earth's orbit has e about 0.017, nearly a circle. Halley's comet has e about 0.97, very stretched.
Dish: parabola. Whisper room: ellipse. Orbit: ellipse. Flyby comet: hyperbola.

ex.q: A whispering gallery is the ellipse x^2/100 + y^2/36 = 1 (units in feet). How far apart must two people stand at the foci?
steps: Read a^2 = 100 and b^2 = 36, so a = 10.
So c = 8 and the foci are (8, 0) and (-8, 0).

dd.trap: Saying planets orbit with the Sun at the center of the ellipse. The Sun is at one focus, not at the middle.
dd.tip: Planets: Sun at a focus, not the middle.

lessons.title: Two ways to name a point · Converting polar to rectangular

cards.h: Two ways to name a point
cards.t: Rectangular coordinates give (x, y). Polar coordinates give (r, θ): how far from the origin and at what angle.

lab.hook: (r, θ): how far and which direction.

cards.t: x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ.
r = √(x² + y²) and tan θ = y/x (check the quadrant).

lessons.title: Polar curves · Parametric equations

cards.t: r = 2 is a circle. r = θ spirals outward. Roses, cardioids and limaçons come from r = a cos(nθ) and similar rules.
Write x and y as functions of a third variable t, like time. They describe motion along a path.
Solve one equation for t and substitute into the other to get a relation between x and y.

lessons.title: The complex plane · De Moivre's theorem

cards.t: Plot a + bi at (a, b). Its modulus is √(a² + b²) and its argument is the angle from the real axis.
In polar form, multiplying complex numbers multiplies the moduli and adds the angles. So (r cis θ)ⁿ = rⁿ cis(nθ).
